The city decided to make Harbor Street safer for bikes! They are turning two lanes into special bike paths starting in March. This is because there were too many bike accidents last year, and this new path will give the many people who ride bikes a safe way to get to the ferry.

However, some shop owners were worried because they might lose parking spots. The city agreed to add six special loading zones to help them out. The whole project will cost a lot of money, and the street will be closed at night for about five weeks while they build it.

Furthermore, the Council has mandated a comprehensive review of the project’s effectiveness after one year, utilizing both crash data and local sales tax receipts to assess the outcome.

Elias frowned. He checked the date. It was Tuesday. He checked the weather forecast. Clear skies.

Imagine a town where the barrier to knowledge isn't the price tag, but the distance to the nearest shelf. I am here today to argue for a simple, yet transformative idea: every town deserves a public tool library.

A tool library is more than just a place to borrow a drill or a ladder. It is an engine for local empowerment. It democratizes access to the means of production. For the aspiring entrepreneur, the DIY homeowner, or the student tackling a complex project, the cost of owning specialized equipment is often prohibitive. A tool library levels that playing field.

Think about the impact. Instead of a neighbor needing a specialized power washer for a weekend project, they can borrow it, learn how to use it, and complete the task. This fosters self-sufficiency, reduces waste, and strengthens our local economy by encouraging home improvement and small-scale innovation.

Furthermore, these libraries become vital community hubs—places where neighbors meet, share skills, and collaborate. They are tangible investments in our collective ingenuity.

Let’s stop viewing tools as mere commodities and start seeing them as catalysts for community growth. Let’s build a town where everyone has the tools—literally and figuratively—to build a better life

The city council voted on Tuesday to convert two lanes of Harbor Street into protected bike lanes starting in March. Supporters said the change would cut crashes, which reached 41 last year on the 1.2 mile stretch, and give the 3,000 daily cyclists a safe route to the ferry terminal. Shop owners worried about losing 60 parking spaces and asked for a loading zone on every block. The council agreed to add six loading zones and to review the plan after one year using crash data and sales tax receipts. The project will cost 2.4 million dollars, most of it from a state grant, and construction will close the street at night for about five weeks. A separate proposal to lower the speed limit to 20 miles per hour on nearby residential streets was delayed until the transportation department finishes a study.
